passage:
The bank's employee counselling room had a box of tissues and a window onto the car park. Reena had used six already.
"Eight months," she said. "Shankar sat next to me for eight months. He brought me tea. He told me about his mother's operation and the hospital bills. I gave him sixty thousand, a bit at a time."
Last week HR had found out that he'd told four other people the same story. His mother was fine. He'd resigned and stopped answering calls.
"I'm a credit officer," Reena said. "I check people's stories for a living. How did I not see it?"
The counsellor said, "People who do this are practised. They study what makes someone kind, and they use that. Being fooled by a skilled liar is not a failing in you. It says he was good at lying, not that you are foolish."
Reena looked at the car park for a long time.

qa.q: How much money did Reena give Shankar?
qa.a: Reena gave Shankar sixty thousand, a bit at a time.

qa.q: Why does Reena feel so ashamed?
qa.a: Reena checks people's stories for a living, so being fooled for eight months makes her question her own judgement and feel foolish.

qa.q: What does the counsellor say that could help Reena?
qa.a: The counsellor explains that practised liars study and use people's kindness, so being fooled says Shankar was skilled at lying, not that Reena is foolish.

qa.q: How might the four other people HR found be feeling?
qa.a: They are probably feeling the same shame and self-doubt as Reena, each thinking they alone should have seen through the story.

grounding: Reena, deceived for months by Shankar, who sat beside her at the bank, feels shame and doubts her judgement, and a counsellor tells her it is not a personal failing.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Dear Anjali,
I've started this letter four times. Here's the truth.
For five months I talked every night to a man I met online who said he was an engineer on an oil rig. He remembered everything I told him. He sent voice notes in the morning. Then his salary got "stuck" and he needed help with a customs fee. I sent money three times.
Last week his photos turned up on a stranger's profile under a different name.
I feel so stupid I can't eat. I'm the one who warns everyone about these things. I keep thinking, how did I miss it?
On Monday I went to the cyber crime cell with every screenshot. The officer read them, then said something I keep repeating to myself: "Madam, he does this every day, to teachers, doctors, even police officers. This is his skill, not your weakness. You did right to come today."
Please call me this weekend.
Mahima

qa.q: How many times did Mahima send money?
qa.a: Mahima sent money three times.

qa.q: Why does Mahima feel so stupid?
qa.a: Mahima usually warns everyone about scams, so being fooled for five months makes her doubt her own judgement and feel deep shame.

qa.q: What did Mahima do that was a strong step after finding out?
qa.a: She took every screenshot to the cyber crime cell and reported it, and she is reaching out to Anjali for support instead of hiding.

qa.q: How did the officer at the cyber crime cell respond?
qa.a: The officer read the screenshots, told Mahima that such people fool teachers, doctors and even police every day, called it his skill, not her weakness, and said she did right to come.

grounding: Mahima, deceived for months online, feels shame and questions her judgement, reports it, and an officer tells her being fooled is not her failing.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Ankita, you keep saying, "How could I be so stupid?" Let me tell you about the time I said those exact words.
When I was twenty-five, a man named Mani joined our office in Coimbatore. He was warm and funny and remembered everyone's children's names. After six months he started a "savings circle". I joined, and I brought in my cousins. For eight months everything looked perfect: receipts, small payouts, tea at his house.
Then one Monday his house was locked and his phone was off. Forty families lost their money.
I couldn't look at my cousins. I told my wife, "Your husband is a fool." For a year I doubted every decision I made.
What pulled me out was a police inspector who said, "Karthik sir, this man has done this in three towns. He is very good at it. Being fooled by a professional is not stupidity; it is his skill."
That was my choice then: to stop punishing myself and start warning others.

qa.q: How many families lost their money?
qa.a: Forty families.

qa.q: How did young Karthik feel after Mani disappeared?
qa.a: Young Karthik felt deep shame, couldn't look at the cousins, called himself a fool and doubted every decision for a year.

qa.q: What turning point inside the story changed Karthik's view?
qa.a: The inspector explaining that Mani had done this in three towns, so being fooled was Mani's skill; after that Karthik stopped self-punishing and started warning others.

qa.q: How might Karthik's cousins have felt about losing their money?
qa.a: The cousins likely felt hurt and angry at the loss, and perhaps at Karthik for bringing them in, which deepened his shame.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling the shame of being deceived for months by a practised con man, and learning it was not a personal failing.

The power had gone out at nine, and Suraj sat in the dark flat with rent due at noon the next day. Manoj's side of the room was empty. So was his cupboard.
For seven months Manoj had said he worked at a bank in Andheri. He'd shown Suraj an ID card, talked about his manager, and borrowed money "till salary day" four times. Tonight Manoj's cousin had called: there was no bank job. There had never been.
Suraj went over it again and again by torchlight. The ID card. The stories. Every time he'd lent money, a small voice had said something was off, and every time he'd ignored it. How could he, an accountant, not see it?
At midnight he called his sister. She listened, then said, "Someone who can lie to your face for seven months without blinking is practised. You trusted a friend. That's not the stupid part."
Suraj didn't feel better yet. But he stopped saying "idiot" out loud.

qa.q: Where did Manoj claim to work?
qa.a: At a bank in Andheri.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling by torchlight?
qa.a: Suraj felt foolish and ashamed, replaying every sign and doubting his own judgement as an accountant.

qa.q: What might help Suraj beyond his sister's call?
qa.a: Talking to the landlord about the rent the next day, writing down what was lent, and reminding himself that practised liars fool careful people too.

qa.q: How does Suraj's sister see what happened?
qa.a: She sees Manoj as a practised liar and Suraj's trust in a friend as normal, not stupid.

grounding: Shows a young man who discovers a flatmate deceived him for months feeling shame and doubting his judgement, and being reminded it is not his failing.

In her PG room in Bengaluru, Bhavna read the message from the cyber cell again. The "Karthik" she had talked to every night for five months, who said he was a naval officer posted at sea, didn't exist. The photos belonged to a fitness trainer in another state. The voice notes came from a number linked to eleven other complaints.
She had never sent him money. He had asked once, for a "medical emergency", and something had made her say no. Still, she felt sick. She had told him about her father's illness, her fears, her salary.
"How did I not see it?" she said to her roommate, Asha.
Asha sat down beside her. "He's done this eleven times, Bhavna. He practises. He's good at it. You were being kind to someone you thought was lonely."
Bhavna laughed, a small cracked sound. She deleted the chat. Then she opened it again, took screenshots of everything for the cyber cell, and deleted it for real.

qa.q: How many other complaints was the number linked to?
qa.a: Eleven other complaints.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel after reading the cyber cell's message?
qa.a: Bhavna felt sick and foolish, doubting her own judgement after sharing her father's illness, her fears and her salary.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that protects her and others?
qa.a: She took screenshots of everything for the cyber cell before deleting the chat, and had already refused his request for money.

qa.q: How does Asha see Bhavna being fooled?
qa.a: Asha sees it as the scammer's practised skill, not Bhavna's failing, since he had done it eleven times and she was being kind.

grounding: Shows a young woman who learns she was deceived for months feeling shame, and being reminded that a practised deceiver fooling her is not her failing.

"Chinmay, I talked to him every night for five months."
"I know, didi."
"Five months. And his photos belong to a wedding photographer in Indore. I found the real man's page today. Same balcony, same dog."
"Did you ever send him anything? Money, pictures?"
"No. He kept saying his account was frozen and maybe I could help. I kept saying later." She pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes. "How did I not see it?"
"Because he was good at it. That was his whole job, apparently. Not yours."
"I'm supposed to be the sensible one. I read everyone's rent agreements!"
"And you still said 'later' every single time he asked for money. That was your sense working."
Nandini gave a wet, shaky laugh. "It doesn't feel like sense. It feels stupid."
"Feeling stupid isn't the same as being stupid. Block him, and we'll report the profile tonight. Then chai."
"Okay. Tonight."

qa.q: Whose photos had the man been using?
qa.a: His photos belong to a wedding photographer in Indore.

qa.q: What is Nandini feeling as she talks to Chinmay?
qa.a: Nandini feels ashamed and foolish, doubting her own judgement because she is 'supposed to be the sensible one'.

qa.q: What small steps does Chinmay suggest for tonight?
qa.a: Block him and report the profile tonight, then sit together over chai, so Nandini acts on it and isn't left alone with the shame.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see what happened to Nandini?
qa.a: Chinmay sees her as the target of a practised deceiver, not a fool, and points out that her repeated 'later' to money requests was good sense.

grounding: Shows a person who finds she was deceived for months feeling foolish, while Chinmay reframes it: being fooled by someone practised at it is not a personal failing.
